paragraphs.heading: Shorter when moving
paragraphs.text: Length contraction means a moving object is measured as shorter than its proper length, which is its length measured in its own rest frame. Its other names, Lorentz contraction and Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction, honour Hendrik Lorentz and George Francis FitzGerald. The shortening shows up only along the direction the object is travelling.

paragraphs.heading: Why you never notice it
paragraphs.text: For everyday objects at everyday speeds, the effect is so tiny it can be ignored for all regular purposes. It only becomes important as the object's speed relative to the observer gets close to the speed of light, usually at a large fraction of it.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring a moving rod
paragraphs.text: Measuring a moving object takes care. One way is to set up a row of clocks and synchronize them, either by trading light signals or by carrying one clock very slowly along the row. Then the object moves past them, and each clock records exactly when its left or right end goes by. Find a clock A that logged the left end and a clock B that logged the right end at the same moment; the distance from A to B is the moving object's length. That makes the meaning of at the same time central to the answer.

paragraphs.heading: Why observers disagree
paragraphs.text: In Newton's mechanics, simultaneity and durations are the same for everyone, so the row-of-clocks method above and a second method, described below, give the same length. In relativity, light's constant speed in all inertial frames, together with time dilation and the relativity of simultaneity, breaks that agreement. An observer who believes they marked both ends at once will be told by observers in other frames that the two marks were not simultaneous. A second method, timing a clock as it travels from one end of the rod to the other, also gives different lengths, because time dilation makes the two travel times differ.

paragraphs.heading: An idea to rescue the aether
paragraphs.text: FitzGerald in 1889 and Lorentz in 1892 proposed the contraction to explain the negative result of the Michelson–Morley experiment and to save the idea of a stationary aether. At the time it was seen as an ad hoc hypothesis, since there was no good reason to think the forces between molecules act like electromagnetic ones. Lorentz pictured a real squeezing of the atoms in an object, with no basic change to space and time. He expected that squeeze to cause measurable strains, but experiments such as Trouton–Noble failed to bear out his expectations.

paragraphs.heading: Einstein and Minkowski
paragraphs.text: In his 1905 paper on special relativity, Albert Einstein removed the ad hoc character of the contraction, called the aether superfluous, and dropped any absolutely stationary space. He proposed that Lorentz's transformation applies to mechanics as well as to electromagnetism. Hermann Minkowski then gave all these relativistic effects a geometric meaning with his four-dimensional spacetime.

paragraphs.heading: What you would actually see
paragraphs.text: How a fast object looks is a separate puzzle, because the contraction mixes with the finite speed of light, and at first this was poorly understood. Lorentz wrongly claimed in 1922 that the effects could be photographed. The difficulties became clear only in 1959, through writing by James Terrell and Roger Penrose on what is now called Terrell rotation. Terrell's paper said a meter stick would appear rotated.
